cells.tense: You're in the middle of it, pen in hand, and you can tell which end of the work belongs to you.
cells.ask: Before the day starts, write down one thing you'll look after and one you'll close, then do them in that order and don't add a third.
cells.core:
You're carrying two or three things that matter and none of them is being crushed. You water what needs watering and step back when it's time, and the stepping back hasn't broken anything. People around you feel the even keel without seeing what it takes to keep it, which is what an even keel is for.

Closing a thing is part of looking after it, not a break from it. You do it without ceremony — shut the laptop on a draft, leave the room while people are still talking, hand a thing back to whoever it actually belongs to. Once, tell someone who's watched you work: 'I'm done with that one.' That's the shape of what's next. What comes back might be a dry patch under something that isn't finished yet.
cells.sheetLine: You look after what's growing and close what's done, and you know which is which.
cells.verb: Tending what's growing with steady, responsible care
cells.place: In the part of a life that opens by letting go of what's finished

cells.tense: You're braced for a future you can't sign for, already living inside a version of this that hasn't arrived.
cells.ask: Pick one unfinished thing and write what finished means for it today, then leave it alone for a day.
cells.core:
You're looking after something that isn't planted yet. The next thing, the after that, the version of this that finally runs itself — you're already leaning into it, and your care has turned into moves made ahead of anything actually there to tend. Nobody ordered the advance. The advance is eating the thing you meant to protect.

When this holds its own, letting go falls out of real finishing — you've sat with the old version long enough that the next one gets a clean floor. Today you're letting go before finishing and calling it readiness. More care won't fix this. The partner's own move might: let the vision be built from what you've actually lived, not from what you're bracing against. One true sentence about what's done teaches you more than the plan for what's not.
cells.sheetLine: You're looking after a planting that hasn't happened yet.
cells.verb: Tending what's growing with steady, responsible care

cells.tense: You're still standing where the release happened, and the floor there has gone quiet under you.
cells.ask: Put one thing you've stopped tending back on the bench for five minutes — one object, one message, one file — and let five minutes be the whole act.
cells.core:
Something you used to look after has gone silent, and you've stopped calling it yours to look after. The bench is still there. You know how to hold two things at once, and today you're holding none, because holding looks like picking the same weight back up — and the weight is the thing that went.

When this is in its power, care happens without strain; you hold space without gripping, and releasing takes nothing from you. Lately the release went first and took the care with it. More effort poured into the bare place won't bring it back — the parent's move will, kept small: stay with what's actually here without asking it to grow yet. Put one hand on one thing and let that be enough. The contact gives you a small true yes about what's still yours.
cells.sheetLine: You've stepped away from the work and you're calling it release.

cells.tense: You're closing things all day without noticing that your hand is the one doing it.
cells.ask: Name one thing you put down this week — out loud, to yourself or one person — and say: 'That one was mine to put down.'
cells.core:
You're already running this — the inbox you don't reopen, the plan you quietly stopped pushing, the thread you stopped pulling. It looks like the situation deciding itself. It isn't. You're the one choosing where the pressure goes, and the choice is going unreported, including to you.

The clean form is the natural one: letting go out of completion, letting a finished thing be finished, letting people see you were the one who finished it. What's missing is the credit going where it belongs. The older, simpler move is available underneath: say the placing-down was yours. Not the reward, not the thank-you. Just the hand. One thing, once, in a sentence someone else could hear. That returns the pen. What comes back afterward isn't the point of picking it up.
cells.sheetLine: Your hand is the one closing, and nobody's been told — including you.
cells.verb: Tending what's growing with steady, responsible care
cells.place: In the part of a life that opens by letting go of what's finished

attempts.check: The active 'you' in each core directly addresses the reader, which the record does not support as a known fact; the house voice uses it throughout, so I follow the same form, but the reader can still decline any line of it. The claim that release and tending are theirs to keep balanced can be answered with 'no, my situation is nothing like this', so each cell leaves the ask doable and useful even if the rest misses. The ask survives being wrong because it's one physical act that yields information no matter the outcome. The sentence that serves the writer most is the Too Little opening — 'Still standing where the letting go happened' — I've made it do one job and then left the room for the reader.
